clinicalPearls: Arises when a fragment of functioning ovarian tissue is left behind after an intended bilateral oophorectomy, later causing pelvic pain or a mass
Should be suspected when a woman develops cyclical pelvic pain, dyspareunia, or an adnexal mass following removal of both ovaries
Premenopausal gonadotrophin and oestradiol levels in a woman said to have had both ovaries removed strongly suggest retained functioning tissue
Risk is greatest after technically difficult surgery with dense adhesions from endometriosis, previous pelvic inflammatory disease, or prior operations
Cross-sectional imaging typically shows a small cystic adnexal lesion adjacent to the pelvic sidewall, often near the ureter
Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision of the remnant, which can be challenging and carries a risk of ureteric injury
Medical suppression of ovarian activity may relieve symptoms temporarily or help localise tissue before surgery but is not curative
reference.pathophysiology: During oophorectomy, particularly when the normal tissue planes are obscured by adhesions or endometriosis, a small portion of ovarian cortex may be inadvertently left in situ. This residual tissue retains its responsiveness to circulating gonadotrophins and continues to undergo follicular activity, forming functional cysts and generating local inflammation and pain. Because the remnant is often buried in scar tissue close to the pelvic sidewall and ureter, it can be difficult to identify and remove completely.
additionalDifferentials: Other adnexal or pelvic sidewall mass
Chronic pelvic pain of non-gynaecological origin
additionalInvestigations: Serum follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone, and oestradiol to demonstrate premenopausal ovarian function
Transvaginal ultrasound to locate a cystic adnexal lesion
Magnetic resonance imaging to characterise and localise the remnant and its relation to the ureter
Tumour markers where malignancy is a concern
Review of prior operative and histopathology records to confirm the extent of previous surgery
redFlags: Imaging or clinical features suggesting malignancy within the mass
Ureteric involvement, hydronephrosis, or obstructive uropathy
Severe or rapidly worsening pelvic pain
Unexpectedly high oestradiol in a patient believed to be surgically menopausal
reference.prognosis: Symptoms usually resolve after complete excision of the remnant, though repeat pelvic surgery through scarred tissue is technically demanding and incomplete removal can lead to recurrence.
pitfalls: Not confirming that the residual tissue is functional before attributing symptoms to it
Underestimating the difficulty and ureteric risk of re-operating in a scarred pelvis
Leaving further tissue behind, resulting in persistent or recurrent symptoms
Confusing ovarian remnant syndrome with a deliberately conserved residual ovary
management: Undertake complete surgical excision of the residual ovarian tissue, ideally by an experienced gynaecological surgeon, as the definitive treatment for the pain and mass
Localise the remnant preoperatively with cross-sectional imaging such as MRI and consider preoperative ureteric stenting to reduce the risk of ureteric injury during dissection through scarred tissue
Offer hormonal suppression with a GnRH agonist or combined oral contraceptive as a temporising or adjunctive measure to quieten follicular activity when immediate surgery is not appropriate
Provide symptomatic analgesia for cyclical pelvic pain and dyspareunia while awaiting definitive treatment
Confirm retained functioning tissue with premenopausal gonadotrophin and oestradiol levels and review of prior operative and histopathology records
Manage within a multidisciplinary team including urology given the remnant's proximity to the pelvic sidewall and ureter, and counsel on the risk of incomplete removal and recurrence
